subject: Cloud Computing
title: Virtual Networks and Isolation
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Virtual Networks and Isolation.

hook.text: Thousands of companies share the same physical network in a data center. How do they stay separate?

buildup.text: Virtual networks create private, isolated spaces on shared hardware — like invisible walls.

discovery.text: Each customer gets their own virtual network with private IP addresses, firewalls, and routing rules.

twist.text: None of this is physical. It's all software pretending to be network hardware.

climax.text: Software-defined networking made the cloud possible. Without it, isolation would require real wires.

punchline.text: Cloud networks are invisible, virtual, and completely real.

quiz.question: What are virtual networks in the cloud?
options: Software-defined isolated network spaces on shared physical hardware
Physical cables that connect only one customer's servers

details.summary: Virtual networks like AWS VPCs and Azure VNets create isolated network environments in the cloud where you control IP addressing, subnets, routing, and access rules. Resources within a virtual network communicate privately, while access from outside is explicitly controlled.
details.whyItMatters: Virtual networks are the foundation of cloud security architecture. Proper network design isolates workloads, controls traffic flow, and creates defense-in-depth security layers.
takeaways: Virtual networks provide isolated environments you fully control
Subnets segment resources into public and private tiers
Security groups and network ACLs control traffic flow

faq.question: What is the difference between public and private subnets?
faq.answer: Public subnets have routes to the internet through an internet gateway, making resources directly accessible from outside. Private subnets have no direct internet route, so resources can only be accessed through load balancers, NAT gateways, or VPN connections.

faq.question: How do security groups work?
faq.answer: Security groups act as virtual firewalls for individual resources. They define which inbound and outbound traffic is allowed by port, protocol, and source. Security groups are stateful, meaning return traffic for allowed connections is automatically permitted. Default is deny all inbound.
